sourceClaimComparison.observation: Both languages preserve locating an image by ray construction from the object's position, starting with individual object points.
Ruler/straightedge and compass remain part of the reflected-path construction; no mirror-equation or numerical task replaces the source purpose.

The axis parallel to AC intersects the focal plane at D, and the reflected path goes through C and D. The later paragraph identifies this as the secondary axis through O, consistently with accepted n70 definitions.
Both versions explicitly restrict the focusing construction to paraxial rays. A self-contained secondary-axis/focal-plane explanation replaces the reader-facing backwards figure-144 citation.

O is explicitly the curvature center. The selected ray lies along the secondary axis and retraces its line after reflection, placing D on both that axis and the focal plane. No thin-lens optical-center rule is substituted.
The A-point image construction and all four convenient ray families remain.

AOC passes through curvature center O and reflected COA retraces the same straight path. This is consistent with radial normal incidence at a spherical surface; no unsupported point substitution occurs.
AFK through the focus is reflected parallel to the principal axis. The paragraph remains under the opening paraxial-approximation restriction, not an arbitrary-aperture focusing claim.
AP strikes the vertex/pole and reflection is symmetric about the principal axis. Vertex and pole denote the same mirror point P in this context.
AE is parallel to the principal axis and reflected EFA1 passes through the focus, within the declared paraxial focusing model.

Both versions restrict common-point convergence to the depicted paraxial imaging model and preserve locating A1 with any two convenient rays. This means a usable distinct pair in that construction, not two copies of the same drawn line.
Other reflected rays share the image point in the same model, while actual mirrors need not reflect every selected special ray. The paragraph does not treat a ray entering a hole as reflected.
The medical concave mirror example and central hole remain. Remaining reflecting surface supplies rays for the image construction. No dimensions, optical power or extra apparatus function is added.
Images of edge/outline points construct the object's image. The highlighted edge identity is retained; this is not rewritten as exactly two object points for every shape.

originalQuestionComparison.observation: Question 1 still asks for the law of reflection. Neither language adds a numerical question or substitutes another task.
Question 2 still asks for the principal focus of a spherical mirror. Its domain is the accepted n70 focus definition; no new all-ray exact-focus assertion is introduced.
Question 3 still asks which rays are convenient for spherical-mirror image construction, preserving the four-ray topic rather than requesting new values or a computed image.
